Subject: Oral Pathology
Question: A union of the roots of adjacent teeth through the cementum is referred to as
Explanation:
[Shafer 7th ed 40, 41/ 6th ed 40]
ConditionExplanation
Gemination• An attempt at division of a single tooth before calcification, resulting in incomplete formation of two teeth.
• The resultant structure will have two completely or incompletely separated crowns with a single root and root canal.
• It is difficult to differentiate between gemination and a case in which there has been fusion between a normal tooth and a supernumerary tooth.
Twinning• The division of a single tooth resulting in one normal and one supernumerary tooth. The number of teeth will be more than normal.
Concrescence• A form of fusion of cementum after completion of root formation.
• The teeth are united by cementum only.
• Maxillary molars are frequently involved.
Fusion• Union of two normally separated tooth germs.
• If the union occurs before calcification, the two teeth are completely united to form a single large tooth.
• If the union occurs after calcification, this is union of roots only. The tooth may have separate or fused root canals.
• Fusion of teeth is more common in deciduous teeth.

Subject: Oral Pathology
Question: Dentinogenesis imperfecta differs from amelogenesis imperfecta in that, the former is
Option B: The result of excessive fluoride ingestion
Option C: The result of faulty enamel matrix formation
Option D: Characterized by calcification of pulp chambers and the root canals of the teeth
Explanation:
[D] [Shafer 7th ed 55/ 6th ed 54-55]
Type IRevised shields classification of dentinogenesis imperfecta
Type I• Dentinogenesis imperfecta is seen without osteogenesis imperfecta.
• Caused by mutation in Dentin sialophosphoprotein (DSPP) gene that maps to chromosome#4.
• Affected teeth are amber brown and opalescent and have broad crowns with constriction of cervical area resulting in ‘Tulip’ shape.
• The teeth have bulbous crowns, with narrow roots and root canals. The pulp chambers are smaller than normal.
• Some researchers found an increase in glycosaminoglycans.
• The dentin is composed of irregular tubules that tend to be larger in diameter and less numerous than normal. This is due to limited ability of odontoblasts to form well organized dentinal matrix.
• The water content in teeth is greatly increased as much as 60% above normal and the micro hardness of dentin closely approximates cementum.
Type II• Also known as Brandywine type or shell teeth (shields type III).
• Apart from DSPP, three other genes, DMP-1, 1BSP and SPP1 are also involved.
• The dentin is extremely thin and the pulp chambers are large due to insufficient and defective dentin formation & multiple pulp exposures are more common than in type I.
• In roentgenograms, the teeth appear as shells of enamel and dentin surrounding extremely large pulp chambers and root canals.
Clinically both types of dentinogenesis imperfecta exhibit a characteristic unusual translucent or opalescent hue. The usual scalloping of DEJ, which tends to form an interlocking union between the enamel and dentin, is absent and this results in early loss of enamel. This results in rapid attrition of enamel and the occlusal surfaces of primary and permanent molars are severely flattened.

Question: Thistle-tube appearance of pulp chamber is a feature of
Explanation:
[A] [Shafer 7th ed 57/ 6th ed 57] Dentin dysplasia (rootless teeth) is characterized by normal enamel but atypical dentin formation with abnormal pulpal morphology.
TypeFeatures
Type I or radicular dentin dysplasia• Both the dentitions are clinically normal.
• The teeth exhibit extreme mobility and are exfoliated prematurely as a result of their abnormally short roots.
• In deciduous teeth, the pulp chambers and root canals are completely obliterated, while in permanent dentition, a crescent shaped pulpal remnant may be seen in the pulp chamber.
• Some times periapical radiolucencies, representing granulomas, cysts, or abscesses involving apparently otherwise intact teeth.
• The pulp is obliterated with calcified tubular dentin, osteodentin and fused denticles.
• Normal dentinal tubule formation appears to be blocked, so that new dentin forms around obstacles and takes the characteristic appearance described as “Lava flowing around boulders” and this pattern of “cascades of dentin” results from repetitive attempts to form root structure.
Type II or Coronal dentin dysplasia• The clinical appearance of permanent dentition is normal, but the deciduous teeth shows brown, opalescent hue as seen in dentinogenesis imperfecta.
• The pulp chambers of deciduous teeth are obliterated as in type I and in dentinogenesis imperfecta.

• The deciduous teeth exhibits amorphous and atubular dentin in radicular portion, while the coronal dentin is normal. The permanent teeth contains multiple pulp stones.

Question: Developmental enamel defects are most commonly seen in
Explanation:
[C] [Shafer’s 7th ed 52/ 6th ed 51] Clinical studies indicate that most cases of enamel hypoplasia involve those teeth that form within the first year of birth, mainly the central and lateral incisors, cuspids and the first molars.

Subject: Oral Pathology
Question: Based on the degree to which apical displacement of the pulpal floor is seen, “Cynodont” is the name given to
Explanation:
[D] [Shafer’s 7th ed 45/ J Indian Soc Pedod Prev Dent: March 2006: Taurodontism of deciduous and permanent molars: Report of two cases] Teeth with pulp chambers that are relatively small and have constriction of the pulp chamber approximately at the CEJ are called as cynodonts. The term taurodontism was introduced by Sir Arthur Keith to describe a dental anomaly where the body of the tooth is enlarged at the expense of the roots (bull-like teeth). The taurodontic teeth are identified by elongated pulp chambers and apical displacement of bifurcation or trifurcation of roots. Due to this, the chamber has a greater apicoocclusal height than in cynodont teeth and lacks the constriction at the level of the CEJ giving it a rectangular shape. Shaw further classified taurodont teeth into hypo, meso and hypertaurodont.
  • Hypotaurodont is the mildest form where the bifurcation/trifurcation is slightly apical to the normal level.
  • Hypertaurodont is extreme form in which the bifurcation/trifurcation occurs near the apices of roots.
  • Mesotaurodont is in between the hypo and hypertaurodont forms.

Subject: Oral Pathology
Question: Fordyce granules mostly occurs in all of the following areas EXCEPT
Explanation:

Fordyce granules are ectopic sebaceous glands that appear as small yellow spots, found frequently in a bilaterally symmetrical pattern on the buccal mucosa, labial mucosa, vermilion border of the lips, retromolar region and occasionally on the tongue, gingiva, frenum and palate. Ectopic sebaceous glands are also found in the esophagus, female and male genitalia, nipples, palms and soles, parotid gland, larynx and the orbit.

Subject: Oral Pathology
Question: Brittle bone syndrome is caused by
Explanation:
[A] [Shafer’s 7th ed 699-700/ 6th ed 694, 695]
Osteogenesis imperfecta, also known as Brittle Bone Disease, or ‘Lobstein syndrome’ is disorder of congenital bone fragility caused by mutations in the genes that codify for type I procollagen. This deficiency arises from an amino acid substitution of glycine to bulkier amino acids in the collagen triple helix structure. If the body does not destroy the improper collagen, the relationship between the collagen fibrils and hydroxyapatite crystals to form bone is altered causing brittleness.
The following 4 types of osteogenesis imperfecta have been reported. Type I - mild form, type II - extremely severe, type III - severe, type IV - undefined. These partly depend on the genetic subtype. Type I and IV are the most common forms of osteogenesis imperfecta.

Subject: Oral Pathology
Question: A 7-year-old child having yellowish discoloured spot of maxillary central incisor. His mother presents a history of injury to deciduous tooth 3 years back with recurrent infections & swelling. The diagnosis is
Explanation:
[A] [Shafer 7th ed 52/ 6th ed 52]
Turner’s hypoplasia is an unusual hypoplasia seen in the permanent maxillary incisors or maxillary or mandibular premolars due to trauma or periapical infection of the deciduous predecessors. The bacterial infection of the periapical tissues may disturb the ameloblastic layer of the permanent tooth and result in a hypoplastic crown. The hypoplasia may range from a mild brownish discolouration to a severe pitting and irregularity of the tooth crown. The affected teeth are called Turner’s teeth.

Subject: Oral Pathology
Question: Marked reduction in amount of dentin, widening of predentin layer, presence of large area of interglobular dentin and irregular pattern of dentin is seen in
Explanation:
[B] [Shafer 7th ed 58/ 6th ed 57]
Regional Odontodysplasia is an unusual anomaly affecting one or several teeth in a localised area, where the shape of teeth may be markedly altered with delay in eruption. The radiographic appearance is ‘ghost appearance’ due to the reduction in the radiodensity of the teeth. The enamel and dentin appear very thin and the pulp chamber is very large. The characteristic histological appearance is marked reduction of dentin, widening of predentin, presence of large interglobular dentin and an irregular pattern of dentin. The other names for this disease are Odontogenic Odontodysplasia, Odontogenesis imperfecta, Odontogenic dysplasia, ghost teeth.

Explanation:

Question: A child has marked difference of crown, root size, eruption pattern of left & right side of jaw. The condition is
Explanation:

Hemifacial hypertrophy or hyperplasia is a rare developmental anomaly characterised by asymmetric growth overgrowth of one or more body parts. An anatomic classification of hemihyperplasia given by Hoyme et al classifies it into complex hemihyperplasia (involvement of half the body), simple hemihyperplasia (involvement of a single limb) or hemifacial hyperplasia (involvement of one side of face). Facial hemihypertrophy is characterised by enlargement on one side of the face, unilateral macroglossia, premature development, eruption and increased size of dentition. Dentition on the hypertrophic side is abnormal in 3 aspects – crown size, root size and rate of development. Permanent teeth may be larger, rate of development and eruption is more rapid along with premature shedding of deciduous predecessors.

Explanation:

The dental manifestations include retardation of tooth eruption, along with increased risk of osteomyelitis (following dental infection/extraction). The teeth are prone to caries. Congenital lack of teeth comprises the most common dental abnormalities in humans. Oligodontia or agenesis of more than six teeth (excluding the third molars), and its less severe form, hypodontia, can be inherited in autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked inheritance mode.
  • Papillon levre syndrome

Subject: Oral Pathology
Question: How will you differentiate between fibrous dysplasia and facial hemiatrophy?
Option B: Distance between the anatomical soft tissue landmarks from midline
Option C: Shape, size and difference in eruption pattern of teeth
Option D: Shape of tooth and supporting structures
Explanation:
[C] [Shafer 7th ed 15, 711]
Facial Hemiatrophy is characterised by progressive wasting of the subcutaneous fat, skin, cartilage, muscle, bone accompanied by contralateral Jacksonian epilepsy, trigeminal neuralgia. The most common sign is a painless cleft, coup de sabre near the midline of the face or forehead that marks the boundary between normal and atrophic tissue. Dental abnormalities include incomplete root formation, delayed eruption; growth of the teeth may also be affected.
Fibrous dysplasia results in expansion and deformity of the jaws and eruption pattern of the teeth may be disturbed due to the loss of normal support of developing teeth or the endocrine disturbances. However the formation of teeth is not affected.

Subject: Oral Pathology
Question: The gene that defines the localization of the tooth germs is
Explanation:

Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) 2,4,7 mRNAs shift between epithelium and mesenchyme during regulation of tooth morphogenesis. Fibroblast growth factor (FGF8, FGF9) have been localised in the dental mesenchyme and act via downstream factors MSX1 and PAX9. Muscle specific homeobox genes MSX-1 and Msx-2, appear to be involved in epithelial mesenchymal interactions and craniofacial development, particularly in the initiation of developmental position (Msx-1) and further development (Msx-2) of tooth buds. Pax-9 is transcription factor necessary for tooth morphogenesis.
